title: Thermal throttle interaction bench diary
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad of experiments that try to reproduce and quantify GPU thermal-throttle interactions with long sustained generation workloads. Goal is pragmatic: detect at what sustained token/s and duty cycles we start to see clock-dropping events and how that maps to tail-latency regressions (p95/p99) for different model variants.

Hardware & env notes (baseline):
- Cluster node types used: 1x A100-80GB (driver 525.105), 1x H100-80GB (driver 535.x), both on the same host image (ubuntu 22.04 + CUDA 12.3).
- Power cap: default (no enforced cap) unless noted.
- Fan control: default server-managed.
- Model: 13B open-weights (GPT2-like arch), fp16 and int8-quantized LLM compiled through our inference backend.
- Runtime: local dev cluster, inference binary v2.7.3-debug, with metrics exported to Prometheus.
- Workload harness: synthetic-token-generator that produces coherent tokens (so kv-cache behavior realistic), uses streaming gRPC call pattern to mimic production.
- Telemetry: nvidia-smi sampling at 1s, nvprof counters (SM clocks, memory clocks), our runtime traces (per-request timings and queue depth), and OS thermal sensors.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Sequence lengths: 64, 256, 1024 (focus on 256 for sustained runs)
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 8
- Concurrency (parallel inflight requests): 1, 8, 16, 32
- Duration per trial: 20 minutes steady-state after warmup (warmup: 2 minutes)
- Quantization: fp16 vs int8 (post-training static quant)

Selected runs (raw observations):
1) A100, fp16, seq256, batch1, conc8 (20m):
   - steady-state tokens/s delivered: ~12.5k tokens/s
   - p50 latency: 85 ms, p95: 210 ms, p99: 430 ms
   - GPU temp: climbed from 62C -> 77C in first 6m then plateaued
   - observed 0 explicit throttle logs from driver, but SM clocks dropped intermittently (3300MHz -> 2850MHz) concurrent with short p99 spikes (~1-2s windows).
   - power draw: 315W avg, occasional peaks 345W
   - notes: latency spikes align with short OS-level cooling fan speed oscillations. Suggest correlation with rack-level air flow.

2) A100, int8, seq256, batch1, conc8 (20m):
   - tokens/s: ~17.8k tokens/s (expected uplift from int8)
   - p50: 68 ms, p95: 165 ms, p99: 390 ms
   - GPU temp: 64C -> 79C
   - found 3 throttle events in nvml (clock policy drop) between minutes 8-12; each event corresponded to 2–4s latency tail blasts (p99 > 1.2s)
   - inference traces show KV-cache flushes a few seconds before spikes — investigate if our memmgr occasionally forces small GC under higher throughput.

3) H100, fp16, seq256, batch1, conc16 (20m):
   - tokens/s: ~35k tokens/s (H100 is ~2.8x A100 for this model/config)
   - p50: 42 ms, p95: 95 ms, p99: 210 ms
   - GPU temp: 58C -> 72C
   - no driver throttle events recorded. Clocks stable.
   - power draw: 280W avg.

4) H100, int8, seq1024, batch4, conc32 (stress run, 20m):
   - tokens/s: ~120k tokens/s
   - p50: 210 ms, p95: 540 ms, p99: 1.6s
   - GPU temp: 70C -> 88C (hit TjMax margin)
   - consistent thermal limit events starting around minute 10, SM clocks downshifted by ~20% during those windows.
   - observed increased PCIe latency (slight) likely due to bus contention under high throughput.

Key patterns & hypotheses:
- H100 shows much higher throughput headroom and fewer throttle events at comparable delivered tokens/s; A100 seems more sensitive to airflow and small oscillations in rack cooling.
- Quantized int8 improves tokens/s but increases sustained power draw and temperatures; this raises probability of thermal-induced clock drops and p99 regressions. There is a trade-off: better median but worse tail under sustained duty cycles.
- Concurrency amplifies the effect: at higher concurrency (con16/32) spikes become longer and more frequent, likely because scheduling/garbage (memmgr/alloc churn) interacts with thermal mitigation windows.
- Some p99 spikes align with short KV-cache maintenance in traces; need to instrument memmgr to rule out GC-induced stalls that coincide with cooling-driven clock drops.

Quick reproducibility checklist (for others):
- Use harness: ./perf-harness --model 13B --quant int8 --seq 256 --batch 1 --conc 8 --duration 1400 --warmup 120
- Start nvidia-smi monitor: watch -n1 nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,power.draw,clocks.sm --format=csv
- Capture runtime traces: export PERF_TRACE=1; ensure prometheus scrape interval <= 5s.

Immediate actions / TODOs:
- [ ] Add a lightweight memmgr debug flag to log small GC/alloc events with timestamps (low perf overhead). Tag: PR-thermal-debug
- [ ] Re-run A100 baseline with forced fan max (if possible) to check airflow hypothesis (coordinate with infra). Target: 2026-02-10.
- [ ] Add a long-duration (2h) low-batch noisy run to see multi-hour steady-state drift.
- [ ] Investigate PCIe saturation traces on H100 run (why does bus latency bump under seq1024+batch4?).
- [ ] Consider a runtime policy that temporarily reduces peak clocks before cooling events to smooth tail (experiment with proactive clock capping).

Open questions / notes to self:
- Are we confident these are thermal events and not power-capping from the host (BMC/BIOS policies)? Need to correlate with host IPMI logs.
- Does our int8 kernel require higher SM clocks to keep latency low; and are we pushing sustained frequency/power envelope harder than fp16? If yes, trading int8 median for tail stability may be acceptable for latency-SLO customers but problematic for SLAs.
- For Dedicated customers (reserved capacity) we should document thermal behavior per GPU SKU in console (predictive tail guidance).

Small ascii table (representative)
Seq | Quant | Conc | tokens/s | p99 | throttle_events
256 | fp16  | 8    | 12500    | 430ms | 0
256 | int8  | 8    | 17800    | 390ms | 3
1024| int8  | 32   | 120000   | 1600ms| many

Footnotes:
- Numbers are noisy; I averaged over two runs for A100 and one for H100 stress runs.
- Keep this doc as a rapidly-updated scratchpad; move cleaned results to Confluence once we lock the memmgr instrumentation.

Quick conclusion (working):
Quantization and concurrency materially increase sustained power/temp. H100 tolerates it better, but on A100 we see intermittent SM-clock drops that map to p99 bursts. Before recommending int8-by-default for cost reasons, we should measure tail risk on representative production duty cycles and document per-SKU guidance.

End of notes.

-- tejas (notes sprinkled with TODOs, do not treat as authoritative yet)
